item.title: Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 for coding, finance and science
item.description: Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, which it describes as its most capable models for coding, finance and science. Fable 5.2 is available now, while Mythos 5.2 is limited to vetted organizations. In pre-release testing cited by Anthropic, Fable 5.2 migrated three complex devices in a day where Claude Sonnet 4.5 managed one, and completed a 30-hour proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. Why it matters for tech: A new top-tier coding model with a published test record gives developers a concrete alternative to compare against current coding models on speed and long-task stamina.

item.title: Meta launches Muse Ember, a small model for agentic coding
item.description: Meta has launched Muse Ember (muse-ember-1.0), a small model built for agentic coding, available through Meta's Models API and Amazon Bedrock, with Azure and Google Cloud to follow. It carries a 1 million token context window and up to 512,000 output tokens, priced at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. On Meta's Intelligence Index benchmark it scored 36 at $0.14 per task, the same score as Claude Haiku at $0.41 per task. Why it matters for tech: A cheaper model that matches a larger rival on Meta's own benchmark puts price pressure on coding agents and widens the choice of small models for everyday coding work.

item.title: Google launches TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max for AI inference and training
item.description: Google has launched two new TPU chips built on its TPU v8 architecture. TPU 8tx is aimed at confidential inference and offers up to two times lower latency than TPU 8t, while TPU 8i Max is aimed at training and fine-tuning and carries twice the compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth of TPU 8i, with two TPU 8i chips in one package. TPU 8tx supports clusters of up to 2,048 hosts with 24 terabits per second of cross-pod bandwidth. Why it matters for tech: New TPU options change the cost and speed trade-off for teams running large models on Google Cloud, and the confidential inference chip addresses regulated workloads that need hardware isolation.

item.title: Diraq installs an 8-qubit silicon spin computer in a Sydney data centre
item.description: Diraq has installed an 8-qubit silicon spin quantum computer at Equinix's data centre in Sydney, which the company describes as the first such system inside a commercial data centre. The system uses under 20 kilowatts and 170 square feet, and Diraq plans to reach up to 256 qubits in the same system within a year. Diraq also published a Quantum at Work report estimating that a 10 percentage point rise in clinical trial success rates could save about $600 million per medicine. Why it matters for tech: Running a quantum system inside a commercial data centre tests whether the technology can operate as a hosted service alongside ordinary cloud hardware instead of in a laboratory.

item.title: IonQ and Carahsoft partner to sell quantum systems to the public sector
item.description: IonQ and Carahsoft have announced a strategic partnership in which Carahsoft becomes IonQ's distributor for the public sector, handling procurement, contract vehicles and resale to federal agencies, higher education and state and local government. The agreement covers quantum computing, networking, sensing and security, and cites Executive Order 14413 on quantum innovation. IonQ points to its Stage C progress in DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative and its quantum network work with the Air Force Research Laboratory in Rome, New York. Why it matters for tech: A dedicated public sector channel puts IonQ's systems in front of government buyers through established procurement routes, which is how most government quantum purchases are made.

item.title: AWS makes AgentCore Runtime V2 generally available in 10 regions
item.description: AWS has made AgentCore Runtime V2 generally available in 10 regions. Sessions now start small and page memory in on demand, and environments are snapshotted once and restored for each instance, holding P75 cold starts at about 2 seconds for images from 200 MB to 2 GB, against about 5.4 seconds rising to nearly 30 seconds on the original runtime. Why it matters for tech: Faster and steadier cold starts remove a common delay for agent workloads that spin up on demand, so teams can run agents without keeping idle capacity warm.

item.title: N-able takes its N-central platform offline after 30 alleged zero-days surface
item.description: N-able has taken its hosted N-central environments offline across the Americas, Europe and Asia-Pacific and told customers running the software on site to shut down their servers, after researcher Sean Bales disclosed more than 30 alleged zero-day flaws in a GitHub repository named Able2Shell. The flaws include authentication bypass, credential disclosure and remote code execution, and the most critical chain used unauthenticated XXE to steal a session, reset a password and run commands as the nable user. N-able said it had not observed active exploitation and is developing a hotfix, with updates every four hours and no return-to-service estimate given. Why it matters for tech: N-central manages IT systems for many small and mid-sized businesses, so taking the platform offline shows how a single disclosure can halt remote management for a large customer base at once.

item.title: SSHole flaw lets attackers bypass login on some Linux systems
item.description: A flaw named SSHole allows authentication bypass in OpenSSH on certain Linux systems built on musl, including Alpine, for accounts whose password hash is the single character "*". An oversized password makes musl return "*", which OpenSSH then treats as a match. Exploitation began on November 5, the day a proof of concept appeared, and OpenSSH 10.6p2 was released the same day as the fix. GreyNoise recorded the first successful exploitation on November 7, with 16 successful chains from 6 source IP addresses. Why it matters for tech: The flaw turns a password length check into a login bypass on affected systems, so administrators running musl-based Linux need the patched OpenSSH version rather than relying on password strength.

item.title: Anthropic spends $3.4 billion on gas turbines to power AI data centres
item.description: Anthropic has agreed to spend $3.4 billion on 1.7 gigawatts of gas-powered generators, taking over Texas supplier OnePWR Solutions' existing Caterpillar orders placed about two years ago. The deal, reached in late September according to Reuters, also covers engineering and construction work. It lets Anthropic sidestep a waitlist for turbines that averages six years in the United States. Why it matters for tech: Securing power generation directly shows that electricity supply, not just chips, now sets the pace for AI data centre expansion, and it ties a leading AI lab to new gas capacity.

item.title: US bars financial institutions from transmitting funds involving crypto exchange MEXC
item.description: The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network has barred US financial institutions from transmitting funds involving MEXC, a Seychelles-based crypto exchange founded in 2018 with more than 40 million users in over 170 countries. Treasury said MEXC was still processing transactions as recently as June 2026 with sanctioned Russian entities Garantex and Grinex. Treasury also said MEXC facilitated or processed at least $226 million in transactions connected to the A7 sanctions-evasion network, which the US Office of Foreign Assets Control has sanctioned. Why it matters for tech: Cutting a large exchange off from the US financial system raises the cost of moving funds through it and signals that crypto venues handling sanctioned flows face direct US action.

item.title: Apple pushes Siri toward agentic tasks, report says
item.description: Bloomberg reports that Apple chief executive John Ternus is pressing AI chief Craig Federighi to speed up the Siri roadmap and deliver an assistant that can act on its own, rivalling OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse. Fine-grained control of Apple's own apps, such as editing photos and organising Safari tabs, is reported to arrive with iOS 27.3, while control of third-party apps, such as placing a food order or booking a table, is reported to follow in the spring. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman writes that Siri could become more like an agent as early as next year. Why it matters for tech: Siri is the assistant built into Apple's devices, so turning it into an assistant that carries out multi-step tasks changes what phone assistants are expected to do.

item.title: Nvidia board opens independent review of chief executive after spy reports
item.description: Nvidia's board of directors said it is opening an independent investigation into chief executive Jensen Huang's relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who US officials believe was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. The board said it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, and that Huang supports the review and will cooperate. The New York Times reported last month on the relationship, which Huang later described as romantic in a memo to staff. Megaspeed, a Nvidia customer, is under a Commerce Department investigation into alleged smuggling of AI chips to China. Why it matters for tech: The review sits where chip export controls meet corporate governance, and its outcome shapes how Nvidia handles foreign-intelligence risk at the top of the company.

item.title: Elvis and Eminem rights holders sue Suno over AI music clones
item.description: Rights holders for Elvis Presley's music and the publisher of some of Eminem's biggest records have sued AI music company Suno, saying it generates music and lyrics that mimic the artists. The Presley suit says Suno violated Tennessee's ELVIS Act, which bars AI companies from cloning a singer's voice. Suno says it prohibits unauthorised use of an artist's work, blocks prompts naming specific artists, and screens uploads for misuse. The suits follow similar claims by Jason Isbell and others in September and add to cases already brought by Sony and Universal Music Group. Why it matters for tech: The cases test whether voice and likeness laws cover AI-generated imitations, a question that decides how music AI tools can be built and sold.

item.title: Perplexity's Teammates keep AI agents working between sessions
item.description: Perplexity has launched Teammates, a system that coordinates several AI agents which remember where past sessions left off and keep working without a new prompt. Shared project state lives in Git, with each project in its own repository and each agent working in a separate sandbox. Perplexity says fewer than 2% of agent submissions are rejected for being based on outdated state, with median submission latency under 1.7 seconds. Teammates is available first on the web for Perplexity Max subscribers, with iOS support planned. Why it matters for tech: Agents that keep working after a tab closes move AI tools from answering questions toward carrying out multi-step work on their own.

item.title: Iris Ohyama breach may have exposed data of 7.7 million people
item.description: Japanese manufacturer Iris Ohyama said personal information belonging to about 7.7 million people may have been exposed after unauthorised access to a third-party cloud service used by its Iris Plaza online store. The company said the impact reaches up to 5.8 million registered and former members and 1.9 million non-members. Names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth and passwords may have been exposed, though passwords for active members were stored encrypted and card data was not in the affected service. As of November 5 the company had received no reports of misuse, and Japan's privacy regulator and police were notified on October 29. Why it matters for tech: A breach through a supplier's cloud service shows customer data can be exposed even when the retailer's own systems are not the entry point.

item.title: Riverlane cuts surface-code logical errors with data-driven decoder fix
item.description: Riverlane has demonstrated a method that finds unmodelled correlated errors directly from syndrome measurement data and folds them into the detector error models used to decode surface-code qubits. The augmented models cut logical error rates by up to 75% in simulations and by 14% on Google's published superconducting hardware data. The approach stays compatible with fast graph-based decoders such as PyMatching, which existing error-correction pipelines already use. Why it matters for tech: Better decoding from measured noise, rather than from theory alone, moves error-corrected quantum computing forward without waiting on new hardware.

item.title: A decision framework for moving autonomous agents from Lambda to EKS
item.description: A senior QA engineer at Amazon describes an autonomous agent that reads test failures, files structured bug reports and catches regressions, running on AWS Lambda for one team at under $5 a month and about 200 invocations a month, saving 8 to 10 hours a week. Scaling the same agent to 50 teams changes the workload from stateless events to long-running, multi-tenant work with shared state and API contention, and the piece sets out when to move to EKS Auto Mode: when a workload needs persistent state, cross-tenant analysis, GPU bursts, namespace isolation and central rate limiting together. At 50 teams the EKS setup is put at roughly $200 to $250 a month in total. Why it matters for tech: The piece gives teams a concrete test for moving agents off serverless, which matters as agent workloads grow from one team to many.

item.title: Docusign turns AI coding tools into an engineering operating model
item.description: Docusign says all of its more than 1,100 engineers are now onboarded to and actively using AI coding tools, after early adoption stalled at 49% of engineers and an 18% productivity gain levelled off. The company credits a six-person Eng AI Champions team and about 75 AI Multipliers embedded in teams, with active usage reaching 93% within two months of the Multipliers starting, and lines of code updated per developer up about 52% from the starting point, though the article notes that volume alone does not prove faster delivery. Internal tools include Kody for coding, Chronicle for observability and DocuWiki for documentation, brought together in Krew, where teams build agents for recurring work under human review; no code enters the system unreviewed. Why it matters for tech: Docusign's numbers show the hard part of AI coding tools is not the rollout but the operating model around them, a lesson other engineering teams are now working through.

item.title: DeepMind AI agents find two weaknesses in retired 1024-bit RSA
item.description: Google DeepMind says AI agents working under human supervision found two weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA encryption, a key size the industry retired years ago. In a sandbox test, the agents reproduced a signature forgery on a solved benchmark key using 3.5 times less CPU time, and a new algorithm improved on the previous best method by roughly 1,600 times in theoretical estimates for short fingerprints, while a second result cuts the average cost of factoring each additional 1024-bit key by about 30 times. DeepMind states modern 2048-bit and larger keys are unaffected and no live systems were touched. Why it matters for tech: AI agents are now doing original cryptanalysis in weeks, so hardness assumptions need continuous re-testing rather than being treated as fixed.

The lab reports a score of 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and says the model is built for long autonomous coding and research tasks. It is available now through the lab's Tinker platform with closed weights, and the lab says it intends to release the full weights under an Apache 2.0 licence next week, after external safety testing and red-teaming. Why it matters for tech: The model is built for hours-long autonomous coding work, and its weights stay closed until safety testing finishes, so the open release is conditional rather than immediate.

item.title: IBM unveils Quantum System Two at the University of Chicago
item.description: IBM, the University of Chicago, the State of Illinois and the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park have unveiled an IBM Quantum System Two in Chicago, the company's first quantum computer in Illinois. The system runs on IBM's Nighthawk processor, a 120-qubit chip, and is hosted at the university's Hyde Park Labs. It anchors the National Quantum Algorithm Center, where researchers from universities, labs and companies work on practical quantum applications, and will move to the new Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park campus once it is built. Why it matters for tech: Putting a 120-qubit system on a university campus gives Illinois researchers local hardware for algorithm work instead of remote cloud access.

item.title: Oxford team simulates Aharonov-Bohm effect with two trapped ions
item.description: Researchers at the University of Oxford have simulated the Aharonov-Bohm effect in a lattice gauge theory using a hybrid trapped-ion quantum computer, in a study published in Nature Physics. Two trapped ions formed a loop with two paths, and entangling the qubits that encode the magnetic flux changed whether a particle could tunnel between sites. When the entangled qubits encoded a nonzero flux, the two paths cancelled out and tunnelling stopped entirely, showing the simulation captures how flux affects particle motion. Why it matters for tech: Simulating gauge theories with matter and flux together moves quantum simulation closer to the physics behind particle interactions and exotic materials.

item.title: AI assisted proof settles a 2008 question about quantum speedups
item.description: A proof by David Turturean of Physical Superintelligence has settled the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, open since 2008, which asks when quantum computers can gain dramatic advantages over classical machines. The proof shows that for yes or no questions on most randomly generated inputs, a classical algorithm can estimate a quantum algorithm’s answer without needing vastly more reads of the input, so large speedups need structure in the problem. The proof was found by an AI research system using a non public Anthropic model on the third day of a run, then checked in the Lean proof assistant and reviewed by researchers. Why it matters for tech: It draws a clearer line around where quantum advantage can come from, pointing algorithm research toward problems with structure worth exploiting.

item.title: OpenSSH ships emergency fix for a flaw that let long passwords bypass login on Alpine Linux

Why it matters for tech: A password check that accepts the wrong input is a serious failure, and Alpine's wide use in containers makes fast patching matter.

item.title: Microsoft: real world exploitation concentrates in a small set of vulnerabilities

item.title: Russia plans underground data centres after Ukrainian drone strikes
item.description: Ars Technica reports that Ukrainian drone strikes on exposed Russian infrastructure have prompted Russian plans to move data centres underground. Russia's Digital Development Ministry has confirmed, as reported by Kommersant, that it completed drone protection recommendations for data centres, covering underground siting for the most critical sites, and sent them to the relevant organisations. Why it matters for tech: The conflict is directly reshaping where and how a major state builds and protects its data centre capacity.
